60094.e: The name comes from a local language and describes the cloud of spray that can be seen from far away. The national park on the Zambian side also has this name.
60094.m: Mosi-oa-Tunya is the local name of Victoria Falls.

60095.q: Which headwater of the Nile supplies most of the Nile water in Egypt during the rainy season?
60095.e: The heavy summer rains in the highlands make the Blue Nile swell. In the past it also brought the fertile mud that fertilised the Nile valley.
60095.m: The Blue Nile supplies most of the Nile flood.

60096.q: Which region in south-western Ethiopia does coffee originally come from?
60096.e: Arabica coffee grows wild in the mountain forests of Kaffa. The region is considered the place of origin of the coffee plant.
60096.m: Coffee comes from the highlands of Kaffa.

60097.q: Which grain with very small seeds is the most important staple food in the Ethiopian Highlands?
60097.e: Teff is used to bake the sour flatbread injera. The plant was domesticated in the highlands.

60098.q: What divides the Ethiopian Highlands into a north-western and a south-eastern part?
60098.e: The Ethiopian Rift is part of the East African Rift System. Several lakes lie in it, including Lake Abaya.
60098.m: The Ethiopian Rift divides the highlands into two halves.

60099.q: What are the Ethiopian Highlands mostly made of?
60099.e: Around 30 million years ago, huge amounts of runny lava poured out. The basalt layers stacked on top of each other form the high plateau today.
60099.m: The Ethiopian Highlands are built of basalt lava.

60100.q: Why do especially many people in Ethiopia live in the highlands rather than the lowlands?
a: The climate there is mild and there is enough rain
There are large oilfields in the highlands
The lowlands lie below sea level
The highlands are free of snow and dry all year
60100.e: At medium altitudes of about 1500 to 2400 m, the Woina Dega, it is neither too hot nor too cold. Grain and coffee grow well there, while the hot lowlands are often too dry.
60100.m: The mild highlands are the most densely populated part of Ethiopia.

60101.q: Which rare predator lives only in the Ethiopian Highlands and hunts mainly rodents there?
60101.e: The Ethiopian wolf lives on Afro-alpine grasslands above about 3000 m. Only a few hundred animals are left.
60101.m: The Ethiopian wolf is one of the rarest species of the dog family.

60102.q: In which months does most rain fall in the Ethiopian Highlands?
60102.e: The main rainy season is called Kiremt and brings most of the year's rainfall. It also makes the Blue Nile swell in summer.
60102.m: In the Ethiopian Highlands it rains mainly in summer.

60103.q: From which lake in the Ethiopian Highlands does the Blue Nile flow?
60103.e: The Blue Nile leaves Lake Tana and soon afterwards plunges over the Tis Issat Falls. The White Nile, on the other hand, comes from Lake Victoria.
60103.m: The Blue Nile flows out of Lake Tana.

60104.q: What is special about the Cape Floristic Kingdom, which includes the area around Cape Town?
a: It is the smallest of the six floral kingdoms
It covers all of Africa south of the Sahara
It consists almost entirely of rainforest
60104.e: The Cape Floristic Kingdom is tiny in area but extremely rich in species. A large proportion of its plant species are found nowhere else.
60104.m: The Cape Floristic Kingdom is the smallest and one of the most species-rich floral kingdoms.

60105.q: What climate does Cape Town have?
60105.e: Cape Town has warm, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. It is one of the few areas with a Mediterranean climate in the southern hemisphere.
60105.m: Cape Town has a Mediterranean climate.

60106.q: Which cape south-east of Cape Town is the southernmost point of Africa?
60106.e: Many people believe the Cape of Good Hope is the southern tip of Africa. In fact Cape Agulhas lies about 150 km further south-east.
60106.m: Cape Agulhas is the southernmost point of Africa.

60107.q: Why is the sea at the beaches on Cape Town's Atlantic side colder than in False Bay?
a: The cold Benguela Current and upwelling water shape the west coast
The Atlantic side lies in the shadow of Table Mountain
Glacial rivers flow into the Atlantic side
False Bay is warmed by volcanoes
60107.e: Off the west coast, cold deep water rises to the surface. False Bay is more sheltered and more influenced by warmer water from the Indian Ocean.
60107.m: Cape Town's Atlantic beaches are cold because of the Benguela Current.

60108.q: Which building in Cape Town is considered the oldest surviving colonial building in South Africa?
60108.e: The five-sided fortress was built by the Dutch East India Company between 1666 and 1679. It replaced an older fort made of clay and wood.
60108.m: The Castle of Good Hope is South Africa's oldest colonial building.

60109.q: Which district of Cape Town was declared a whites-only area under apartheid, after which about 60,000 residents were driven out?
60109.e: From 1966 the residents were forcibly removed and the houses demolished. Today a museum remembers the district.
60109.m: District Six stands for the forced removals of apartheid.

60110.q: Which flowers are typical of the fynbos around Cape Town and provide South Africa's national flower?
60110.e: The king protea is South Africa's national flower. Proteas shape the fynbos, the hard-leaved vegetation of the Cape, and can be seen, for example, in Kirstenbosch botanical garden at Table Mountain.
60110.m: The protea is South Africa's national flower.

60111.q: What rock is the upper part of Table Mountain made of?
60111.e: The horizontal sandstone layers lie on top of granite and shale. Because the hard sandstone weathers slowly, the flat plateau has survived.
60111.m: Table Mountain has a cap of hard sandstone.

60112.q: What nickname does Cape Town have because the first European city in southern Africa was founded here?
60112.e: As the oldest city in South Africa, Cape Town is seen as the country's “mother city”. Johannesburg, on the other hand, is called the “City of Gold”.
60112.m: Cape Town is called the Mother City.

60113.q: Which river rises in the Rocky Mountains and shaped the Grand Canyon?
60113.e: The Colorado River rises in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. Over millions of years it cut up to 1800 m deep into the rock in Arizona.
60113.m: The Colorado from the Rocky Mountains shaped the Grand Canyon.

60114.q: What is the warm, dry downslope wind on the eastern side of the Rocky Mountains called, which makes snow melt quickly in winter?
60114.e: The chinook is a foehn-like downslope wind: the air warms up dry-adiabatically as it descends. It can make the temperature rise sharply within hours, similar to the foehn in Switzerland.
60114.m: The chinook is the foehn of the Rocky Mountains.

60115.q: Which line of longitude is traditionally seen as the rough boundary between the wetter east and the dry western Great Plains?
60115.e: The 100th meridian west roughly marks the line beyond which rainfall is usually no longer enough for farming without irrigation. West of it, grazing land and irrigation dominate.
60115.m: The 100th meridian west roughly separates the wet from the dry part of the Great Plains.

60116.q: Which irrigation method creates the typical circular fields of the Great Plains that you can see from an aeroplane?
60116.e: In centre pivot irrigation, a long sprinkler arm turns around a central well. This creates circular green fields.
60116.m: Centre pivot irrigation creates round fields in the Great Plains.

60117.q: Which US law of 1862 gave settlers 160 acres of land if they farmed it?
60117.e: The Homestead Act of 1862 gave 160 acres (about 65 ha) to settlers who farmed the land for five years. It strongly encouraged the settlement of the Great Plains.
60117.m: The Homestead Act of 1862 brought many settlers to the Great Plains.

60118.q: Which tributary of the Mississippi is the longest?
60118.e: The Missouri is longer than the Mississippi above their confluence. Together, the Missouri and Mississippi form one of the longest river systems in the world.
60118.m: The Missouri is the longest tributary of the Mississippi.

60119.q: Into which river channel would the Mississippi probably shift its main course without the Old River Control Structure?
60119.e: The Atchafalaya offers a shorter, steeper route to the Gulf of Mexico. Since the 1960s the Old River Control Structure has prevented the Mississippi from switching there.
60119.m: The Old River Control Structure keeps the Mississippi away from the Atchafalaya.

60120.q: What do you call a river loop cut off by the Mississippi that remains as a crescent-shaped lake?
60120.e: When a meander is broken through, the old loop is separated from the main channel. An oxbow lake forms.
60120.m: A cut-off meander becomes an oxbow lake.

60121.q: What forms every summer off the mouth of the Mississippi because of fertiliser from farming?
60121.e: Nitrate and phosphate from the fields encourage algal blooms. When the algae decompose, the oxygen in the water is used up, creating a dead zone (hypoxia).
60121.m: Fertiliser from the Mississippi causes a dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico.

60122.q: What are the natural ridges parallel to the river called that the Mississippi builds up during floods by depositing sand on its banks?
60122.e: When the river overflows its banks, the water immediately slows down and drops coarse material right at the bank. This creates natural levees, which are often higher than the floodplains behind them.
60122.m: During floods a river builds its own natural levees.

60123.q: What is the effect called in which cold air over the open Great Lakes picks up moisture and brings a lot of snow to the eastern shores?
60123.e: Cold polar air picks up heat and moisture over the warmer lake water. On the downwind shore it drops this again as snow in heavy bands, for example in Buffalo.
60123.m: The lake effect brings a lot of snow to the eastern shores of the Great Lakes.

60124.q: From which geological era do most of the rocks of the Canadian Shield date?
60124.e: The Canadian Shield consists mainly of Precambrian rocks such as gneiss and granite. It is the ancient core of the North American continent.
60124.m: The rocks of the Canadian Shield are Precambrian.

60125.q: Which mining town in Ontario lies in an ancient meteorite crater with rich nickel deposits?
60125.e: The Sudbury Basin was created by an impact about 1.85 billion years ago. It is one of the most important nickel and copper deposits in the world.
60125.m: Sudbury lies in an impact crater full of nickel ore.

60126.q: In geology, what do you call an old, stable continental core like the Canadian Shield?
60126.e: A craton is a part of the continental crust that has been stable for a very long time. Its parts exposed at the surface are called a shield.
60126.m: The Canadian Shield is the exposed part of a craton.

60127.q: Roughly how old is the Acasta Gneiss in the Canadian Shield, one of the oldest known rocks on Earth?
60127.e: The Acasta Gneiss in the Northwest Territories has been dated to about 4 billion years. It is one of the oldest known rocks in the Earth's crust.
60127.m: The Acasta Gneiss is about 4 billion years old.

60128.q: Which energy source is used on a large scale on the Canadian Shield in Quebec, for example in the James Bay Project?
60128.e: The many lakes and steep rivers over hard rock are ideal for reservoirs. That is why Quebec produces most of its electricity from hydroelectric power.
60128.m: A lot of hydroelectric power is produced on the Canadian Shield in Quebec.

60129.q: Which ice mass is the largest in the southern hemisphere outside Antarctica?
60129.e: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field stretches for about 350 km along the Andes between Chile and Argentina. Many large outlet glaciers flow from it.
60129.m: The Southern Patagonian Ice Field is the largest ice mass in the southern hemisphere after Antarctica.

60130.q: Which plateau on Earth is larger than the Altiplano?
60130.e: The Altiplano is considered the second largest plateau in the world. Only the Tibetan Plateau is more extensive.
60130.m: The Altiplano is the second largest plateau on Earth after Tibet.

60131.q: On which Caribbean island did the capital Plymouth have to be abandoned from 1995 because of eruptions of the Soufrière Hills volcano?
60131.e: The eruptions of the Soufrière Hills buried Plymouth under ash and mudflows. The south of Montserrat is still an exclusion zone today.
60131.m: On Montserrat the capital Plymouth was abandoned because of a volcano.

60132.q: On which island is Pitch Lake, the largest natural asphalt deposit in the world?
60132.e: Pitch Lake in the south of Trinidad is a lake of natural asphalt. Trinidad also has important oil and natural gas reserves.
60132.m: Pitch Lake on Trinidad is a natural asphalt lake.

60133.q: Which feature on the surface of Yucatán traces the rim of the buried impact crater?
60133.e: The cenotes in north-western Yucatán form a striking semicircle. It follows the crater rim because the rock there is more fractured and dissolves into karst more easily.
60133.m: A ring of cenotes marks the rim of the Chicxulub crater.

60134.q: Above roughly what sea surface temperature can hurricanes form?
60134.e: Hurricanes get their energy from evaporation over warm water of at least about 26 °C. That is why the warm Gulf of Mexico is an ideal breeding ground.
60134.m: Hurricanes need sea water of at least about 26 °C.

60135.q: Which scale divides hurricanes into five categories according to their wind speed?
60135.e: The Saffir-Simpson scale goes from Category 1 to 5. The Fujita scale, on the other hand, is for tornadoes, and the Beaufort scale for wind in general.
60135.m: Hurricanes are rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

60136.q: Why do practically no hurricanes form right at the equator?
a: The Coriolis force there is almost zero
The sea there is too cold
The wind there always blows from the west
The air there is too dry
60136.e: A tropical storm needs the Coriolis force to spin. At the equator it is almost zero, so hurricanes usually only form from about 5 degrees of latitude.
60136.m: Without the Coriolis force no hurricane can spin.

60137.q: Why did the 1985 earthquake cause so much damage in Mexico City, even though the epicentre was about 350 km away on the Pacific coast?
a: Soft lake sediments amplified the waves
The city lies directly on a plate boundary
A volcano erupted at the same time
60137.e: The waterlogged clays of the former lake made the earthquake waves build up, rather like a jelly. Medium-height buildings in particular collapsed.
60137.m: Soft lake beds amplify earthquake waves.

60138.q: Which weather situation makes smog worse in Mexico City because the basin surrounded by mountains traps the air?
60138.e: In an inversion, warm air lies above colder air near the ground and prevents the air from mixing. Exhaust fumes then build up in the basin, similar to winter under the low cloud on the Swiss Plateau.
60138.m: An inversion traps smog in the Mexico City basin.

60139.q: What are the artificial garden islands in the canals of Xochimilco called, an Aztec farming method?
60139.e: Chinampas are fields built up from mud and plants in shallow lake water. They are very fertile and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60139.m: Chinampas are Aztec garden islands in Xochimilco.

60140.q: What do you call a city like Mexico City that far outstrips all other cities in the country in population and importance?
60140.e: A primate city dominates its country's system of cities in economy, politics and culture. The Mexico City metropolitan area is many times larger than Guadalajara or Monterrey.
60140.m: Mexico City is a typical primate city.

60141.q: Where does Tierra del Fuego get its name from?
a: From the fires of the indigenous people
60141.e: In 1520 Magellan's sailors saw many fires and columns of smoke made by the local people on the coast. This gave rise to the name “Tierra del Fuego” (Land of Fire).
60141.m: Tierra del Fuego is named after the fires of the indigenous people.

60142.q: What was the name of the indigenous people who lived on the main island of Tierra del Fuego as hunters of guanacos?
60142.e: The Selk'nam (also called Ona) hunted guanacos on the main island. Through persecution and introduced diseases, they were almost wiped out in the late 19th century.
60142.m: The Selk'nam were the indigenous people of the main island of Tierra del Fuego.

60143.q: Which animal, introduced from North America in 1946, now badly damages the forests of Tierra del Fuego?
60143.e: Argentina released beavers in 1946 to build up a fur industry. Without natural enemies they multiplied rapidly and destroy the southern beech forests with their dams.
60143.m: Introduced beavers damage the forests of Tierra del Fuego.

60144.q: What is the name of the strait between Cape Horn and the Antarctic Peninsula?
60144.e: The Drake Passage is about 800 km wide and known for its high seas. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows through it.
60144.m: The Drake Passage lies between South America and Antarctica.

60145.q: Who mediated between Chile and Argentina in the Beagle conflict over three islands near Tierra del Fuego, which ended with a peace treaty in 1984?
60145.e: In 1978 Chile and Argentina were close to war over the islands of Picton, Lennox and Nueva. Pope John Paul II mediated, and the peace treaty was signed in 1984.
60145.m: The Pope mediated in the Beagle conflict.

60146.q: In which mountain range is Pikes Peak in Colorado, which inspired the song “America the Beautiful”?
60146.e: Pikes Peak belongs to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains in Colorado. After climbing it, Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem “America the Beautiful” in 1893.
60146.m: Pikes Peak is in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado.

60147.q: What is the name of the easternmost mountain range of the Rocky Mountains in Colorado, at whose foot Denver and Boulder lie?
60147.e: The Front Range rises abruptly out of the Great Plains. Colorado's large cities are lined up along its foot.
60147.m: The Front Range is the first mountain range of the Rockies coming from the east.

60148.q: Which mountain, at about 3954 m, is the highest peak in the Canadian Rocky Mountains?
60148.e: Mount Robson in British Columbia towers almost 3000 m above its surroundings. Mount Logan is higher, but it is in the Saint Elias Mountains in the Yukon.
60148.m: Mount Robson is the highest mountain in the Canadian Rockies.

60149.q: What is special about the meltwater of the Columbia Icefield in the Canadian Rocky Mountains?
a: It seeps completely into the karst
It flows only into the Pacific
It feeds a lake with no outflow
60149.e: Three drainage basins meet at the Columbia Icefield. Its meltwater reaches the Pacific, the Atlantic via Hudson Bay and the Arctic Ocean via the Mackenzie.
60149.m: The Columbia Icefield drains into three oceans.

60150.q: Which famous fossil site with finely preserved soft-bodied animals from the Cambrian lies in Yoho National Park?
60150.e: The Burgess Shale is well over 500 million years old. It shows animals of the Cambrian explosion including their soft parts, which is very rare.
60150.m: The Burgess Shale shows living things from the Cambrian.

60151.q: Which pest has killed huge pine forests in the Rocky Mountains and British Columbia since the 1990s?
60151.e: The mountain pine beetle bores under the bark of pine trees. Mild winters, in which the larvae do not freeze to death, favoured its mass spread.
60151.m: Mild winters helped the mountain pine beetle in the Rocky Mountains.

60152.q: What is the name of the largest grass-covered dune area in North America, in the Great Plains?
60152.e: The Sandhills in Nebraska are old sand dunes that are now held in place by prairie grass. Beneath them lies an important part of the Ogallala groundwater.
60152.m: The Sandhills in Nebraska are dunes held in place by grass.

60153.q: What do you call the deeply cut, almost bare erosion landscapes in South Dakota?
60153.e: In the Badlands, rain and runoff quickly wear away soft layers of sediment and ash. This creates gullies, ridges and colourful layered walls.
60153.m: Badlands are landscapes furrowed by erosion.

60154.q: Which very flat plateau in the south of the Great Plains lies in Texas and New Mexico?
60154.e: The Llano Estacado is one of the flattest large areas in North America. It is bordered by steep slopes, the “Caprock Escarpments”.
60154.m: The Llano Estacado is a flat plateau in Texas and New Mexico.

60155.q: Which isolated upland in the Great Plains is sacred to the Lakota and bears the Mount Rushmore memorial?
60155.e: The Black Hills rise like an island out of the prairie of South Dakota. For the Lakota they are a sacred place, and their ownership is still disputed today.
60155.m: The Black Hills are a sacred upland of the Lakota.

60156.q: Which very fertile soil type with a thick, humus-rich top layer is typical of the tallgrass prairie?
60156.e: A lot of humus builds up under the dense root mat of the grasses. This creates black earth (chernozem), one of the most fertile soils in the world.
60156.m: Fertile black earth formed under the prairie.

60157.q: In which year did the great Mississippi flood happen, after which the USA completely reorganised its flood protection?
60157.e: In the 1927 flood many levees broke, and hundreds of thousands lost their homes. The Flood Control Act of 1928 handed flood protection to the federal government.
60157.m: The Mississippi flood of 1927 changed flood protection in the USA.

60158.q: How was the upper Mississippi above St. Louis made navigable for large barge tows?
60158.e: A chain of dams with locks keeps a minimum water depth. This allows barges to carry grain from the Midwest downstream.
60158.m: Locks and dams make the upper Mississippi navigable.

60159.q: What is the Bonnet Carré Spillway above New Orleans for?
a: It diverts Mississippi floodwater into Lake Pontchartrain
It produces electricity for New Orleans
It keeps sea water out of the Mississippi
It serves as a lock for cruise ships
60159.e: The Bonnet Carré Spillway is a relief structure. When it is opened during floods, part of the Mississippi flows into Lake Pontchartrain and the water level at New Orleans drops.
60159.m: The Bonnet Carré Spillway protects New Orleans from Mississippi floods.

60160.q: Which main reason contributes to the Mississippi Delta in Louisiana losing land every year?
a: Dams and levees hold back sediment
The river carries more and more sand
Sea level in the Gulf is falling
60160.e: Dams trap sediment, and levees stop the river from bringing mud onto the marshes. At the same time the ground is sinking, so coastal land is lost.
60160.m: Without new sediment the Mississippi Delta shrinks.

60161.q: Which canal bypasses Niagara Falls and connects Lake Erie and Lake Ontario for ships?
60161.e: The Welland Canal uses locks to overcome a difference in height of about 100 m. It is a key part of the St. Lawrence Seaway.
60161.m: The Welland Canal takes ships past Niagara Falls.

60162.q: Which invasive parasite almost wiped out the lake trout populations in the upper Great Lakes in the 20th century?
60162.e: The sea lamprey attaches itself to fish and feeds on their blood. It reached the upper lakes through shipping canals.
60162.m: The sea lamprey badly harmed the fish of the Great Lakes.

60163.q: Which introduced mussel spread explosively in the Great Lakes from the late 1980s?
60163.e: The zebra mussel came from Europe in ballast water. It clogs water pipes and changes the food web, and it is also widespread in Swiss lakes.
60163.m: The zebra mussel came to the Great Lakes in ballast water.

60164.q: What happened to the Chicago River around 1900 so that Chicago's sewage no longer flowed into Lake Michigan?
a: Its direction of flow was reversed
It was diverted into Lake Ontario
60164.e: Since the building of the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, the river has flowed away from the lake towards the Mississippi. This kept the drinking water from the lake cleaner.
60164.m: The Chicago River has flowed backwards since 1900.

60165.q: Why is a remote island well suited to studying the relationship between wolves and moose?
a: Hardly any animals arrive or leave
There are no diseases on islands
Wolves only hunt at night on islands
Islands always have a mild climate
60165.e: On Isle Royale in Lake Superior, wolves and moose have been observed since 1958. Because hardly any animals arrive or leave, the population changes of predator and prey can be studied well.
60165.m: Wolves and moose are studied on Isle Royale.

60166.q: Which smaller lake, not counted as one of the five Great Lakes, lies between Lake Huron and Lake Erie?
60166.e: The water of Lake Huron flows via the St. Clair River into Lake St. Clair and then via the Detroit River into Lake Erie. The lake is only a few metres deep.
60166.m: Lake St. Clair connects Lake Huron and Lake Erie.

60167.q: Which river near Cleveland, flowing into Lake Erie, caught fire in 1969 and became a symbol of the environmental movement?
60167.e: Oily waste on the Cuyahoga River caught fire in 1969. The event contributed to the Clean Water Act of 1972.
60167.m: The burning Cuyahoga River helped promote water protection in the USA.

60168.q: What is still happening today to the land around Hudson Bay as a result of the last Ice Age?
a: It is folding up into mountains
60168.e: The enormously heavy ice sheet pressed the Earth's crust down. Since the ice disappeared, the crust has been slowly springing back, and old shorelines now lie far above the sea.
60168.m: Around Hudson Bay the land is rising after the Ice Age.

60169.q: What are the widespread bog and swamp areas on the Canadian Shield called?
60169.e: Muskeg forms in hollows with poor drainage over impermeable rock. It makes building roads and railways very difficult.
60169.m: Muskeg is the bogland of the north.

60170.q: Which mine in the Northwest Territories, opened in 1998, was Canada's first diamond mine?
60170.e: The diamonds of the Ekati mine come from kimberlite pipes in the old rock of the Shield. This made Canada an important diamond producer.
60170.m: Ekati was Canada's first diamond mine.

60171.q: Which range of hills in Minnesota on the southern Canadian Shield is the most important iron ore region in the USA?
60171.e: The Mesabi Range has supplied iron ore since the late 19th century. It was shipped across Lake Superior to the steelworks.
60171.m: The Mesabi Range is the iron ore district of the USA.

60172.q: What is the name of the long-distance road, built from 1976, that opens up remote Chilean Patagonia?
60172.e: The Carretera Austral runs through the fjords, rainforest and glacial valleys of southern Chile. Before that, many places could only be reached by ship.
60172.m: The Carretera Austral opens up Chilean Patagonia.

60173.q: What was found in 1907 in the Patagonian coastal town of Comodoro Rivadavia while drilling for drinking water?
60173.e: A borehole that was actually supposed to find drinking water struck oil in 1907. Comodoro Rivadavia thus became the starting point of the Argentine oil industry.
60173.m: Argentina's oil age began in Comodoro Rivadavia.

60174.q: What is the name of the huge shale formation in Neuquén from which oil and natural gas are extracted by fracking?
60174.e: Vaca Muerta is one of the largest shale gas and shale oil deposits in the world. It has greatly increased Argentina's energy production.
60174.m: Vaca Muerta is Argentina's large shale oil field.

60175.q: Which cave in Patagonia (Argentina) is known for handprints on the rock walls that are thousands of years old?
60175.e: Some of the hand outlines in the Cueva de las Manos in Santa Cruz Province are about 9000 years old. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60175.m: Ancient handprints can be seen in the Cueva de las Manos.

60176.q: Which wild camel is the typical large animal of the Patagonian steppe?
60176.e: The guanaco lives in herds in the steppes of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. It is adapted to cold, wind and sparse food.
60176.m: The guanaco is the wild camel of Patagonia.

60177.q: Where is the lowest point in South America, about 105 m below sea level?
a: Mouth of the Amazon in Brazil
60177.e: Laguna del Carbón lies in a basin with no outflow in the Argentine province of Santa Cruz. It is the lowest point in the southern and western hemispheres.
60177.m: The lowest point in South America is in Patagonia.

60178.q: Which gigantic dinosaur was discovered in the Patagonian province of Neuquén?
60178.e: Argentinosaurus was a huge plant-eater from the Late Cretaceous. It is considered one of the largest land animals known.

60179.q: Which mining town on the edge of the Altiplano became one of the richest cities in the world in the 16th century thanks to the silver mountain Cerro Rico?
60179.e: The silver of Cerro Rico financed large parts of the Spanish colonial empire. Many indigenous forced labourers died in the mines.
60179.m: The silver of Potosí made Spain rich.

60180.q: Which city on the Bolivian Altiplano is known for its carnival, recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage?
60180.e: The Carnival of Oruro combines Catholic festivals with Andean traditions, such as the devil dance Diablada. UNESCO recognised it in 2001.
60180.m: The Carnival of Oruro is UNESCO cultural heritage.

60181.q: Which large lake on the Bolivian Altiplano dried up almost completely in 2015?
60181.e: Shallow Lake Poopó lost almost all its water through drought, water extraction and high evaporation. Fishermen lost their livelihoods.
60181.m: Lake Poopó almost dried up in 2015.

60182.q: Which means of transport has connected La Paz with higher-lying El Alto since 2014?
60182.e: The Mi Teleférico cable car network crosses the steep valley basin where the roads are jammed. It is considered the largest urban cable car network in the world and was built by the Doppelmayr/Garaventa Group, which includes the Swiss company Garaventa.
60182.m: In La Paz the cable car is a means of public transport.

60183.q: Which large city lies at about 4000 m directly on the high plain of the Altiplano above La Paz?
60183.e: El Alto lies above the valley basin of La Paz and has grown rapidly, mainly through migration from rural areas. La Paz airport is also here.
60183.m: El Alto is one of the highest large cities in the world.

60184.q: Which volcano on the western edge of the Altiplano, at about 6540 m, is the highest mountain in Bolivia?
60184.e: Nevado Sajama is an extinct stratovolcano. Queñua trees grow on its slopes, forming some of the highest forests in the world.
60184.m: Sajama is the highest mountain in Bolivia.

60185.q: Between which two mountain ranges does the Altiplano lie?
a: Eastern and Western Cordillera of the Andes
60185.e: The Altiplano is a high basin between the Cordillera Occidental and the Cordillera Oriental. It was filled with debris eroded from the mountains.
60185.m: The Altiplano lies between two Andean ranges.

60186.q: On which Caribbean island did La Soufrière volcano erupt explosively in April 2021, after the north had been evacuated in time?
60186.e: The eruption of La Soufrière covered St Vincent in ash. Thanks to early warning by volcano monitoring, hardly anyone was killed.
60186.m: La Soufrière on St Vincent erupted in 2021.

60187.q: What is Kick 'em Jenny, north of Grenada in the Caribbean?
60187.e: Kick 'em Jenny lies under the sea a few kilometres off the coast. When activity increases, an exclusion zone for ships is set up.
60187.m: Kick 'em Jenny is an underwater volcano near Grenada.

60188.q: Which Caribbean island has been a “special municipality” of the Netherlands since 2010?
60188.e: Since the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles in 2010, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba have belonged directly to the Netherlands. Aruba and Curaçao are separate countries within the Kingdom.
60188.m: Bonaire is a special municipality of the Netherlands.

60189.q: Which small Caribbean island is divided between France and the Kingdom of the Netherlands?
60189.e: The north is called Saint-Martin and belongs to France, the south, Sint Maarten, to the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The division goes back to a treaty of 1648.
60189.m: St Martin is divided between France and the Netherlands.

60190.q: What are the Bahamas made of geologically, unlike many volcanic Lesser Antilles?
60190.e: The Bahamas lie on flat carbonate banks of limestone that built up over millions of years from marine organisms. Blue holes, collapsed karst caves, are typical.
60190.m: The Bahamas are built of limestone.

60191.q: Where is the deepest point of the Atlantic, at a depth of about 8400 m?
60191.e: The Puerto Rico Trench lies north of Puerto Rico on the boundary between the Caribbean and North American plates. It also poses an earthquake and tsunami risk.
60191.m: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest point of the Atlantic.

60192.q: What is the name of the cave system near Tulum in Quintana Roo that is considered the longest explored underwater cave system in the world (as of 2026)?
60192.e: Ox Bel Ha is a huge network of water-filled karst passages under the Yucatán Peninsula. By early 2026 more than 540 km of underwater passages had been surveyed.
60192.m: Ox Bel Ha is the longest known underwater cave system in the world.

60193.q: What is the clearly visible boundary layer called where divers in the karst waters of Yucatán pass from fresh water into the salt water below?
60193.e: The lighter fresh water floats on top of the sea water seeping in. At the halocline the water shimmers like heat above a road.
60193.m: At the halocline fresh water meets salt water.

60194.q: Uxmal on the Yucatán Peninsula is a ruined city of which civilisation?
60194.e: Uxmal lies in the hilly Puuc region south of Mérida. It is known for the Pyramid of the Magician and the richly decorated Maya mosaic façades.
60194.m: Uxmal is a Maya ruined city on Yucatán.

60195.q: Which fibre plant brought Yucatán great wealth around 1900 because ropes and twine were made from it?
60195.e: The henequen agave supplied sisal fibres for ship ropes and binder twine. The plantation owners became rich, while the Maya workers often lived in debt bondage.
60195.m: The henequen agave made Yucatán rich around 1900.

60196.q: Which people rose up in the Caste War from 1847 on the Mexican Yucatán Peninsula?
60196.e: In the Caste War, the Maya fought against the rule of whites and mestizos. Independent Maya areas existed in the east of the peninsula for decades.
60196.m: The Caste War was a long Maya uprising on Yucatán.

60197.q: What is the name of the railway line opened at the end of 2023 that serves the Yucatán Peninsula in a ring?
60197.e: The Tren Maya is meant to promote tourism and development. Critics point to damage to forest, caves and cenotes.
60197.m: The Tren Maya is a ring railway on Yucatán.

60198.q: Which biosphere reserve on the Caribbean coast of Yucatán, with mangroves, lagoons and reefs, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
60198.e: Sian Ka'an includes rainforest, wetlands and part of the coral reef. It was added to the World Heritage list in 1987.
60198.m: Sian Ka'an protects Yucatán's coastal landscapes.

60199.q: What happens to the name of an especially devastating hurricane?
a: It is given to the next storm
It becomes the name of a category
It is passed on to another sea
60199.e: The World Meteorological Organization removes the names of very destructive storms from the name lists. They are replaced with new names.
60199.m: Names of terrible hurricanes are retired.

60200.q: What is it called when a hurricane's wind speed increases by at least about 55 km/h within 24 hours?
60200.e: Rapid intensification often happens over very warm water with little wind shear. It is dangerous because there is little time left for evacuations.
60200.m: Rapid intensification makes hurricanes suddenly strong.

60201.q: Which warm ocean current in the Gulf of Mexico can make hurricanes especially strong?
60201.e: The Loop Current brings warm Caribbean water through the Yucatán Channel into the Gulf. Its warm layer goes deep, so a storm hardly cools the water.
60201.m: The Loop Current gives hurricanes in the Gulf a lot of energy.

60202.q: Which hurricane brought record rain of more than 1500 mm in 2017 and flooded large parts of Houston?
60202.e: After making landfall in Texas, Harvey stayed almost still for days. As a result, an extreme amount of rain fell in the Houston area.

60203.q: Which condition in the atmosphere often prevents a tropical storm from becoming a hurricane?
60203.e: With strong wind shear, wind direction or speed changes a lot with height. This tears the vortex apart and stops it from building up vertically.

60204.q: What do many strong Atlantic hurricanes that later reach the Gulf of Mexico develop from?
60204.e: Many hurricanes start as disturbances in the easterly flow, known as African easterly waves. They move west across the warm Atlantic and strengthen.
60204.m: Many hurricanes begin as waves off West Africa.

60205.q: How has the Basin of Mexico, which originally had no outflow, been protected from flooding since colonial times?
a: With artificial drainage canals and tunnels
With a dam in the south
By pumping water into the ground
60205.e: Because the high valley had no natural outflow, the Spanish already dug drainage ditches. Today canals and tunnels carry the water away to the north.
60205.m: The Basin of Mexico is drained artificially.

60206.q: With which measure has Mexico City tried to reduce air pollution since 1989?
a: Driving bans depending on the number plate
A ban on all petrol cars
A city toll for lorries only
60206.e: Under the “Hoy No Circula” programme, cars may not be driven on certain days depending on the last digit of their number plate. Air quality has improved since then.
60206.m: Mexico City fights smog with “Hoy No Circula”.

60207.q: Which Aztec temple complex was excavated in the centre of Mexico City in 1978 after a huge stone relief was found?
60207.e: In 1978 workers found the stone of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui. After that, the main temple of Tenochtitlan was uncovered next to the cathedral.
60207.m: The Templo Mayor lies in the middle of Mexico City.

60208.q: On the ruins of which Aztec capital was Mexico City built?
60208.e: Tenochtitlan lay on an island in Lake Texcoco. After the Spanish conquest in 1521, Mexico City was built in its place, and the lake was gradually drained.
60208.m: Mexico City stands on the remains of the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan.

60209.q: How does the border between Chile and Argentina run on the main island of Tierra del Fuego?
60209.e: On Isla Grande the border follows a straight line along a meridian. The west belongs to Chile, the east to Argentina.
60209.m: On Tierra del Fuego the border follows a line of longitude.

60210.q: Where did the Yaghan, considered one of the southernmost peoples in the world, live?
a: In Tierra del Fuego at the southern tip of South America
60210.e: The Yaghan lived as canoe nomads on the coasts south of the main island of Tierra del Fuego. In 2022 Cristina Calderón, the last native speaker of their language, died.
60210.m: The Yaghan are a people from Tierra del Fuego.

60211.q: Which Chilean town on Navarino Island disputes Ushuaia's title of southernmost city in the world?
60211.e: Puerto Williams lies south of Ushuaia on the Beagle Channel. Because it is much smaller, it is disputed whether it counts as a city.
60211.m: Puerto Williams lies even further south than Ushuaia.

60212.q: According to its full name, which areas does the Argentine province of Tierra del Fuego also claim?
60212.e: The province is called “Tierra del Fuego, Antártida e Islas del Atlántico Sur”. This includes Argentina's claims to part of Antarctica and to islands such as the Falkland Islands.
60212.m: The province of Tierra del Fuego also includes Argentina's claims to Antarctica.

60213.q: Which watershed does the Great Dividing Range form in south-eastern Australia?
a: Short coastal rivers in the east, the Murray-Darling system in the west
Rivers to the Indian Ocean in the east, to the Pacific in the west
Glacial rivers in the north, desert rivers in the south
Rivers to the Gulf of Carpentaria in the east, to the Tasman Sea in the west
60213.e: On the eastern side, short, steep rivers flow straight into the Pacific. To the west, long rivers such as the Darling drain into the Murray-Darling Basin.
60213.m: The Great Dividing Range separates the coastal rivers in the east from the Murray-Darling system in the west.

60214.q: Which mountain area west of Sydney was long seen as an obstacle and was crossed in 1813 by Blaxland, Lawson and Wentworth?
60214.e: The Blue Mountains with their steep sandstone gorges long blocked the settlers in Sydney from reaching the interior. The 1813 expedition followed the ridges instead of the valleys and so found the way west.
60214.m: Only in 1813 did settlers manage to cross the Blue Mountains west of Sydney.

60215.q: Which large water engineering project (1949 to 1974) diverts water from the mountains of the Great Dividing Range to the west and produces electricity?
60215.e: The Snowy Mountains Scheme carries water from the Snowy River through tunnels to the western side of the mountains. There it is used for irrigation in the Murray-Darling Basin and drives hydroelectric power stations.
60215.m: The Snowy Mountains Scheme combines hydroelectric power with irrigation inland.

60216.q: Roughly how long is the Great Dividing Range, which stretches from Queensland to Victoria?
60216.e: The range stretches for about 3500 km along the east side of Australia. This makes it the longest mountain range on the continent, but it is relatively low.
60216.m: At about 3500 km, the Great Dividing Range is Australia's longest mountain range.

60217.q: Why is the Great Dividing Range relatively low despite its length?
a: It is very old and heavily eroded
It consists only of young volcanoes
It lies in a zone without uplift
It is constantly flooded by the sea
60217.e: Australia lies in the middle of a plate, far from active collision zones. The range is geologically old, has been eroded over a very long time and therefore only reaches just over 2000 m.
60217.m: Old mountain ranges far from plate boundaries are usually heavily eroded and rather low.

60218.q: Which organisation, founded in 1928, brings medical help by aeroplane to remote farms in the Outback?
60218.e: The minister John Flynn founded the Flying Doctor Service in 1928. Doctors still fly to people who live hundreds of kilometres from the nearest hospital.
60218.m: In the Outback the doctor often comes by aeroplane, thanks to the Royal Flying Doctor Service.

60219.q: How did children on remote Outback farms receive lessons from 1951 in Alice Springs?
a: By radio in the School of the Air
Only in state boarding schools on the coast
By letters that came monthly by ship
60219.e: The School of the Air first used the radio network of a medical flying service. Today the distance lessons run via the internet and satellite.
60219.m: The School of the Air makes distance learning possible for children in the vast Outback.

60220.q: Which type of farming shapes large parts of the Outback, with properties larger than some Swiss cantons?
60220.e: Because the land is dry and little grass grows, each animal needs a very large area. That is why the stations are huge; the largest, Anna Creek, covers about 24,000 km².
60220.m: In the dry Outback a cow needs a very large area of pasture.

60221.q: Which desert is the largest in Australia by area?
60221.e: The Great Victoria Desert lies in Western Australia and South Australia. It consists mainly of sandhills, grassland and salt pans.
60221.m: Australia's largest desert is the Great Victoria Desert.

60222.q: Roughly what share of Australia's area does the Murray-Darling Basin cover?
60222.e: The basin covers about one million square kilometres. That is about one seventh of the country's area and about 25 times the area of Switzerland.
60222.m: The Murray-Darling Basin covers about one seventh of Australia.

60223.q: Which environmental problem arose in the Murray-Darling Basin through land clearing and intensive irrigation?
60223.e: After deep-rooted trees were cleared and through irrigation, salty groundwater rose. The salt reached soils and rivers and harmed farming and ecosystems.
60223.m: Land clearing and irrigation can bring salty groundwater to the surface.

60224.q: What is the Murray-Darling Basin Plan of 2012 mainly meant to achieve?
a: Less water extraction, so that rivers and wetlands keep enough water
The building of a canal to the Pacific
Diverting the Murray into the interior
60224.e: The plan sets sustainable limits on water extraction. To do this, the government buys back water rights from farmers, among other things.
60224.m: The Murray-Darling Basin Plan is meant to balance farming and river ecosystems.

60225.q: What is the long dry period called that hit south-eastern Australia from about 1997 to 2009 and made the Murray drop sharply?
60225.e: During the Millennium Drought, river flows and reservoirs fell to record lows, and the mouth of the Murray had to be dredged. The drought led to reforms of water policy.
60225.m: The Millennium Drought showed how vulnerable the Murray-Darling system is.

60226.q: Why does the Darling often carry little water compared with its length?
a: It flows through dry land with high evaporation
It is fed entirely by glaciers
It seeps away into a karst mountain range
It is diverted into a neighbouring country
60226.e: The Darling crosses semi-arid areas where hardly any rain falls and a lot of water evaporates. In addition, a lot of water is taken for irrigation, so at times it dries up.
60226.m: Rivers in dry areas lose a lot of water through evaporation.

60227.q: Which geological structure runs along the Southern Alps on New Zealand's South Island?
a: The Alpine Fault as a plate boundary
An old rift valley with no movement
60227.e: Along the Alpine Fault the Pacific and Australian plates slide past each other and are pushed together. This is why the Southern Alps are still rising today.
60227.m: New Zealand's Southern Alps form at the Alpine Fault between two plates.

60228.q: Why is New Zealand's North Island more volcanically active than the South Island?
a: There the Pacific Plate dives beneath the Australian Plate
There is a hotspot in the middle of the plate there
Two plates are breaking apart there
60228.e: East of the North Island the Pacific Plate is subducted and melts at depth. The rising magma feeds the Taupō Volcanic Zone with volcanoes such as Ruapehu and Tongariro.
60228.m: Subduction under the North Island supplies the magma for New Zealand's volcanoes.

60229.q: Which national park on the North Island, founded in 1887, was New Zealand's first?
60229.e: The Māori chief Te Heuheu Tūkino IV gave the sacred peaks to the state so that they would be protected. Today the park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for nature and culture.
60229.m: Tongariro National Park is New Zealand's oldest national park.

60230.q: Why does much more rain fall on the west coast of the South Island than on the Canterbury Plains in the east?
a: Westerly winds drop their rain on the Alps
The west coast is closer to the equator
Sea ice prevents rain in the east
60230.e: Moist westerly winds rise over the Southern Alps and bring the west coast several metres of rain a year. In the lee to the east it is dry, and a warm downslope wind often blows.
60230.m: New Zealand's Southern Alps create a rain shadow in the east.

60232.q: Roughly how high above sea level is Tuvalu's highest natural point?
60232.e: Tuvalu consists only of flat atolls and reef islands. With a highest point of about 4.6 m, it is one of the flattest countries on Earth.
60232.m: Tuvalu is so flat that even small changes in sea level are a threat.

60233.q: What is the capital of Tuvalu?
60233.e: Funafuti is an atoll where the government and about 60 per cent of the population live. Tarawa is the capital of Kiribati, Majuro that of the Marshall Islands.
60233.m: The capital of Tuvalu is the atoll of Funafuti.

60234.q: How does seawater getting in harm farming on Tuvalu?
a: Salt gets into the groundwater and the pulaka pits
The seawater makes the soil freeze
The seawater brings toxic volcanic ash
The seawater washes away all the coconut palms
60234.e: On atolls a thin lens of fresh water floats on the salt water. If the sea level rises or storm surges come, the groundwater and the growing pits for the root crop pulaka become salty.
60234.m: On atolls salt water threatens the thin freshwater lens in the ground.

60235.q: What did a 2018 study find about the land area of Tuvalu's islands since the 1970s?
a: The land area had increased slightly overall
The land area had stayed exactly the same
60235.e: The study compared aerial photographs from 1971 to 2014: the land area increased overall by about 2 to 3 per cent. Waves and storms move sand and coral rubble around, but the risk from flooding and salinisation remains.
60235.m: Reef islands can shift, but sea level rise remains a great danger.

60236.q: How many atolls and reef islands make up the country of Tuvalu?
60236.e: Tuvalu means roughly “eight standing together”, because originally eight islands were inhabited. In total the country consists of nine atolls and reef islands with only about 26 km² of land.
60236.m: Tuvalu consists of nine small islands and atolls.

60237.q: Which unusual source of income does Tuvalu have thanks to its internet country code?
a: Licences for undersea cables to Asia
60237.e: The .tv ending is popular with television and streaming companies. The licence fees make up an important part of the national budget.
60237.m: Tuvalu earns money from the internet ending .tv.

60238.q: What does the Madrid Environmental Protocol (1991) to the Antarctic Treaty ban?
a: Any mining of mineral resources except for research
All scientific drilling into the ice
60238.e: The protocol declares Antarctica a natural reserve devoted to peace and science. Mining is banned, and a review is possible at the earliest 50 years after it came into force, so from 2048.
60238.m: The Madrid Protocol bans mining in Antarctica.

60239.q: Which of these countries makes a territorial claim in Antarctica?
60239.e: Seven countries make claims: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. Several claims overlap, especially on the Antarctic Peninsula.
60239.m: Seven countries make territorial claims in Antarctica, including Norway.

60240.q: Roughly what share of all the ice on Earth is in the Antarctic ice sheet?
60240.e: The Antarctic ice sheet is by far the largest mass of ice on Earth. It also stores most of the world's fresh water.
60240.m: About nine tenths of the Earth's ice lies in Antarctica.

60241.q: What do ice cores such as the one from Dome C in East Antarctica show?
a: The climate and composition of the air over the last 800,000 years or so
The temperature of the Earth's core
The age of the continental plates
The water temperature of the deep sea today
60241.e: Ancient atmosphere is trapped in air bubbles in the ice. From this, CO₂ levels and temperatures over eight ice age cycles can be read, with the University of Bern also taking part.
60241.m: Ice cores are a climate archive with trapped ancient air.

60242.q: Who was the first to sail the entire Northeast Passage, in 1878/79 on the ship Vega?
60242.e: The Finnish-Swedish explorer Nordenskiöld sailed from Sweden along the Siberian coast to the Pacific. Shortly before the end, the Vega had to spend the winter stuck in the ice.
60242.m: In 1878/79 Nordenskiöld was the first to conquer the Northeast Passage.

60243.q: Which two seas or straits does the Northeast Passage connect?
60243.e: The Northeast Passage runs along the northern coast of Europe and Asia from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It crosses the Kara Sea, the Laptev Sea and the East Siberian Sea, among others.
60243.m: The Northeast Passage runs north of Russia from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

60244.q: Why are shipping companies interested in the Northeast Passage as a route between Europe and East Asia?
a: It is much shorter than the route through the Suez Canal
It is completely free of ice all year
It has no territorial waters of any country
It is the only route without fees
60244.e: Between northern Europe and Japan or China, the sea route is shortened by about a third depending on the destination. However, ice, the cost of icebreakers and a lack of ports make the route risky.
60244.m: The Northeast Passage is shorter but harder than the route through the Suez Canal.

60245.q: Which cape is the northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland and a key point of the Northeast Passage?
60245.e: Cape Chelyuskin lies on the Taymyr Peninsula on the Vilkitsky Strait. The ice there is often especially stubborn.
60245.m: The northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland is Cape Chelyuskin.

60246.q: Which ships does Russia use to keep the Northeast Passage open even in thick ice?
60246.e: Russia is the only country that operates a fleet of nuclear-powered icebreakers. They can sail for a long time without refuelling and break thick pack ice.
60246.m: Nuclear icebreakers keep the Northeast Passage open for cargo ships.

60247.q: Which seafarer spent the winter of 1596/97 on Novaya Zemlya while searching for a sea route to Asia?
60247.e: Willem Barents' expedition got stuck in the ice and spent the winter in a hut made of driftwood. Barents died on the return journey, and the Barents Sea is named after him.
60247.m: Willem Barents searched for the Northeast Passage in the 16th century.

60248.q: Why has the Northeast Passage become navigable for longer each year in recent decades?
a: Arctic sea ice is shrinking sharply in summer
New canals have been dug through Siberia
The Bering Strait has been widened
60248.e: Because the Arctic is warming, the area of summer sea ice has fallen sharply. This opens the route for longer but brings risks for the environment and climate.
60248.m: The decline of sea ice makes the Northeast Passage navigable for longer.

60249.q: What is the Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Greenland, known for?
a: A very fast glacier calves huge icebergs there
The highest mountain in Greenland is there
The oldest Viking settlement is there
60249.e: The Sermeq Kujalleq glacier pushes huge amounts of ice into the fjord every year. The icebergs then drift out into Disko Bay.
60249.m: In the Ilulissat Icefjord one of the fastest glaciers in the world calves.

60250.q: How did Tasmania become an island?
a: After the last Ice Age the sea level rose and flooded the land bridge
A volcanic eruption blasted it off the mainland
An earthquake made Bass Strait suddenly sink
It drifted away from the mainland as a separate plate
60250.e: During the last Ice Age the sea level was much lower and Tasmania was joined to the mainland. About 10,000 to 12,000 years ago the land bridge was flooded.
60250.m: The rise in sea level after the Ice Age made Tasmania an island.

60251.q: Which disease has seriously threatened the Tasmanian devil since the 1990s?
60251.e: Devil Facial Tumour Disease is passed from animal to animal through bites. As a result, the populations have collapsed.
60251.m: A contagious facial cancer threatens the Tasmanian devil.

60252.q: In which year did the last known thylacine die in a zoo in Hobart?
60252.e: The thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger, was wiped out by hunting, loss of habitat and disease. The last animal died in Beaumaris Zoo in 1936.
60252.m: The thylacine has been considered extinct since 1936.

60253.q: What did a large protest movement prevent in the Tasmanian wilderness in 1982/83?
a: The building of a dam on the Franklin River
The building of a nuclear power station
The opening of a gold mine
The building of a bridge to the mainland
60253.e: Thousands protested against the building of a dam on the Franklin River in the World Heritage area, and over 1000 were arrested. In July 1983 the High Court of Australia ruled in favour of the federal government, which stopped the building.
60253.m: The Franklin Dam protest was a milestone of environmental protection in Australia.

60254.q: Which energy source supplies most of the electricity in Tasmania?
60254.e: Lots of rain and mountainous land make Tasmania ideal for reservoirs and hydroelectric power stations. As in Switzerland, hydroelectric power is the most important source of electricity there.
60254.m: Tasmania gets its electricity mainly from hydroelectric power.

60255.q: Which raw material is most important for the economy of New Caledonia?
60255.e: New Caledonia has a large share of the world's known nickel deposits. Nickel is used, among other things, for stainless steel and batteries.
60255.m: New Caledonia is rich in nickel.

60256.q: What was the result of the three independence referendums in New Caledonia in 2018, 2020 and 2021?
a: A no to independence each time
A yes to independence each time
All were cancelled because of unrest
60256.e: In all three votes New Caledonia stayed with France. The last one was boycotted by many Kanak, so the question remains disputed.
60256.m: New Caledonia voted three times against independence from France.

60257.q: Under which special form of rule was Vanuatu, as the New Hebrides, until 1980?
a: Joint administration by Britain and France
60257.e: The New Hebrides were a British-French condominium with two administrations and legal systems. In 1980 Vanuatu became independent.
60257.m: Vanuatu became independent from Britain and France in 1980.

60258.q: What did the people of Bougainville vote for in 2019 with about 98 per cent?
60258.e: The vote was part of the peace agreement after the civil war over the Panguna copper mine. It is not binding, and independence still has to be negotiated.
60258.m: Bougainville voted clearly for independence in 2019.

60259.q: How did Polynesian seafarers find their way to distant islands over thousands of kilometres without a compass?
a: Using stars, wave patterns, birds and clouds
60259.e: Traditional navigation used the rising points of stars, ocean swell, bird flights and clouds over islands. The voyage of the canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 proved that this works.
60259.m: Polynesians navigated by stars, waves and birds.

60260.q: Which volcanic eruption in January 2022 triggered a tsunami and a pressure wave that could be measured worldwide?
60260.e: The undersea volcano near Tonga exploded with enormous force. The pressure wave was also recorded by barometers in Switzerland.
60260.m: The eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Haʻapai could be measured worldwide.

60261.q: Why is Kiribati the only country that lies in all four hemispheres?
a: It lies on both sides of the equator and the 180th meridian
It lies on both sides of the prime meridian
It stretches from the North Pole to the equator
It has territory in Europe and Asia
60261.e: Kiribati's islands are spread over a huge area of ocean north and south of the equator and east and west of the 180th meridian. That is why the country moved the date line to the east in 1995.
60261.m: Kiribati lies in all four hemispheres of the Earth.

60262.q: What consequences did phosphate mining have for the island of Nauru?
a: About four fifths of the island is destroyed mining land
The island became twice as large
The island became a nature reserve
60262.e: Phosphate from bird droppings made Nauru very rich for a time. After mining, an uninhabitable plateau of limestone rock remained, and the wealth was lost.
60262.m: Phosphate mining has made most of Nauru uninhabitable.

60263.q: What is special about the traditional stone money (rai) on Yap?
a: The huge stones change owner without being moved
The stones are fired again every year
It is only kept under water
60263.e: The rai stones were brought from Palau and can be several metres across. Ownership is passed on by word of mouth, while the stone stays where it is.
60263.m: With Yap's stone money, ownership counts, not where the stone is.

60264.q: Which ruined city made of basalt columns on Pohnpei has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016?
60264.e: Nan Madol consists of almost a hundred artificial islands in a lagoon. It was the centre of the Saudeleur dynasty.
60264.m: Nan Madol on Pohnpei is a ruined city in the sea.

60265.q: What were the stick charts of the Marshall Islands used for?
a: They showed wave patterns and the position of islands for navigation
They were calendars for the fishing season
They served as money in trade
They showed the constellations for ceremonies
60265.e: The charts made of palm ribs and shells showed how islands break and bend the ocean swell. Seafarers learned them by heart on land.
60265.m: Stick charts of the Marshall Islands show ocean waves and islands.

60266.q: What is most of the water from the Murray-Darling Basin used for?
60266.e: A large part of Australian farming takes place in the basin, for example rice, cotton, fruit and wine. Irrigation uses most of the water that is taken.
60266.m: The Murray-Darling Basin is Australia's breadbasket.

60267.q: Which strait separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland?
60267.e: Bass Strait is about 240 km wide and relatively shallow. The Torres Strait lies between Australia and New Guinea, Cook Strait in New Zealand.
60267.m: Bass Strait separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland.

60268.q: What is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia?
60268.e: Palikir lies on the island of Pohnpei and has been the capital since 1989. Majuro is the capital of the Marshall Islands, Ngerulmud that of Palau and Hagåtña that of Guam.
60268.m: Palikir on Pohnpei is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia.

60269.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site on the slopes of the Great Dividing Range protects rainforests with plant lineages dating from the time of the supercontinent Gondwana?
60269.e: The protected areas are scattered across New South Wales and southern Queensland. They contain plant families that already existed when Australia was still joined to Antarctica.
60269.m: The Gondwana Rainforests are living witnesses of an ancient supercontinent.

60270.q: What consequence did the crossing of the Blue Mountains in 1813 have for the British colony?
a: Grazing land in the interior was opened up
Sydney was abandoned as the main town
Large gold finds were made at once
60270.e: West of the mountains the settlers found wide grasslands. A road soon followed, then the town of Bathurst in 1815, and sheep farming spread.
60270.m: After 1813 settlers opened up the pastures west of the Blue Mountains.

60271.q: Which rock is needed for caves with stalactites and stalagmites like those in the Blue Mountains?
60271.e: Rainwater with dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves limestone and creates hollow spaces. When the water drips in the cave, the lime is deposited again and forms stalactites and stalagmites, for example in the Jenolan Caves.
60271.m: Caves with stalactites form in limestone.

60272.q: Who is the train “The Ghan”, which connects Adelaide with Darwin via Alice Springs, named after?
60272.e: In the 19th century camel drivers from Afghanistan and British India carried goods through the Outback. The train remembers them with its name and a camel in its logo.
60272.m: The name “The Ghan” remembers the Afghan camel drivers in the Outback.

60273.q: What made crossing Australia from south to north especially dangerous in the 19th century?
a: Lack of water and great heat
60273.e: Expeditions had to travel hundreds of kilometres without reliable water sources. John McDouall Stuart managed the crossing in 1862 and returned alive; the Stuart Highway follows his route.
60273.m: The Stuart Highway follows the route of the explorer John McDouall Stuart.

60274.q: Which inselberg in the centre of Australia is a sacred place of the Aboriginal people?
60274.e: Uluru, formerly Ayers Rock, rises about 350 m out of the flat plain. It is sacred to the Anangu, and since 2019 it may no longer be climbed.
60274.m: Uluru is a sacred mountain of the Aboriginal people in the Outback.

60275.q: How did the Burke and Wills expedition of 1860/61, which wanted to cross Australia from south to north, end?
a: The leaders died on the way back
They found a large inland lake
They founded the city of Darwin
60275.e: The expedition reached the mangrove swamps on the Gulf of Carpentaria. On the way back Burke and Wills starved to death, even though Aboriginal people gave them food for a time.
60275.m: The Burke and Wills expedition shows how dangerous the Outback was for the unprepared.

60276.q: Why is the Murray regulated with large reservoirs?
a: So that water flows to fields and towns even in the dry summer
So that the river does not freeze in winter
So that ocean-going ships can sail inland
So that the river carries more sand to the sea
60276.e: In Australia river flow varies greatly. Reservoirs such as Lake Hume store water from wet periods and release it in dry periods.
60276.m: Reservoirs even out the changing amount of water in the Murray.

60277.q: Why is the name “Milford Sound” geographically not quite accurate?
a: It is a fjord shaped by glaciers
It is the crater of a volcano
It is a lagoon behind a reef
It is a river delta with sandbanks
60277.e: A “sound” is a river valley flooded by the sea. Milford Sound, however, was carved out by glaciers and is therefore a fjord.
60277.m: Despite its name, Milford Sound is a fjord.

60278.q: What is the name of New Zealand's third largest island, south of the South Island?
60278.e: Stewart Island lies across Foveaux Strait. About 85 per cent of the island belongs to Rakiura National Park, which is known for kiwis.
60278.m: New Zealand's third largest island is Stewart Island.

60279.q: On which main island of New Zealand does the great majority of the population live?
a: On the North Island, about three quarters
On the South Island, about three quarters
On the South Island, about two thirds
60279.e: Auckland, the largest city, and the capital Wellington are on the North Island. The larger South Island is more mountainous and more thinly populated.
60279.m: Most New Zealanders live on the North Island.

60280.q: What were Tuvalu's islands called when they were part of a British colony?
60280.e: Together with the Gilbert Islands, today's Kiribati, Tuvalu formed the colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands. Tuvalu became independent in 1978.
60280.m: In colonial times Tuvalu was called the Ellice Islands.

60281.q: What did Tuvalu set down in a change to its constitution in 2023?
a: The state continues to exist even if its land sinks into the sea
Tuvalu becomes part of New Zealand
Only English is an official language
60281.e: The constitution declares Tuvalu's statehood and its maritime borders to be permanent. In this way the country wants to secure its rights even if the islands become uninhabitable.
60281.m: Tuvalu wants to continue existing as a state even without habitable land.

60282.q: In which city has the Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty been based since 2004?
60282.e: The permanent secretariat organises the annual consultative meetings and manages information. Argentina successfully won the bid to be the host country.
60282.m: The Antarctic Treaty Secretariat is in Buenos Aires.

60283.q: Which 1980 convention in the Antarctic Treaty System regulates fishing, especially for krill?
a: Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
60283.e: The convention (CCAMLR) looks at the whole ecosystem, not just individual fish species. It is meant to prevent krill being fished so heavily that penguins, seals and whales go hungry.
60283.m: CCAMLR protects the ecosystem of the Southern Ocean from overfishing.

60284.q: Which sea area was declared the largest marine protected area in the world at the time under CCAMLR in 2016?
60284.e: The protected area in the Ross Sea covers more than 1.5 million square kilometres. Commercial fishing is banned in a large part of it.
60284.m: One of the largest marine protected areas in the world is in the Ross Sea.

60285.q: Which large area of Antarctica is not claimed by any country?
60285.e: Marie Byrd Land in West Antarctica is the largest unclaimed land area on Earth. Because of the Antarctic Treaty, no new claim may be made to it either.
60285.m: Marie Byrd Land is the largest area with no territorial claim.

60286.q: What must a country that joined later prove in order to become a consultative party with voting rights?
a: A coast on the Southern Ocean
Membership of the UN Security Council
60286.e: Under Article IX, substantial research activity is needed, such as a station of its own or expeditions. Without this status a country may take part in meetings but not in decisions.
60286.m: Voting rights in the Antarctic Treaty go to those who do serious research there.

60287.q: Roughly how thick is the Antarctic ice sheet on average?
60287.e: On average the ice is about 2 km thick, and much more in the thickest places. That is why Antarctica is the continent with the highest average elevation.
60287.m: The Antarctic ice sheet is about two kilometres thick on average.

60288.q: What are the cold, heavy winds called that flow down from the high ice sheet to the coast?
60288.e: Over the ice the air cools strongly, becomes heavy and flows downhill to the coast. At some coastal places these downslope winds reach hurricane force.
60288.m: Katabatic winds are cold downslope winds from the ice sheet.

60289.q: Under the ice of East Antarctica lies a mountain range about as extensive as the Alps. How was it discovered?
a: By measurements that see through the ice
By finding pieces of rock on the coast
60289.e: The Gamburtsev Mountains lie beneath more than 600 m of ice. They were discovered in 1958 by seismic measurements of a Soviet expedition and later surveyed more precisely with radar.
60289.m: The Gamburtsev Mountains are hidden beneath the ice of East Antarctica.

60290.q: What do you call fast-flowing bands in the ice sheet that carry a large part of the ice to the sea?
60290.e: Ice streams flow much faster than the surrounding ice, often hundreds of metres a year. The ice sheet loses a large part of its mass through them.
60290.m: Ice streams are the motorways of the ice sheet.

60291.q: Why are especially many meteorites found in Antarctica?
a: Flowing ice collects them on blue ice areas at the surface
Antarctica is hit more often than other continents
The magnetic field pulls meteorites towards the South Pole
Meteorites melt into the ice and stay visible
60291.e: The ice carries trapped meteorites to places where wind wears the ice away. On these blue ice areas the dark stones lie clearly visible.
60291.m: Blue ice areas in Antarctica are ideal places to find meteorites.

60292.q: Which raw material is shipped from the Siberian Yamal Peninsula via the Northeast Passage with icebreaking tankers?
60292.e: On the Yamal Peninsula natural gas is extracted, liquefied and taken to Europe and Asia by icebreaking tankers. The port of Sabetta was built especially for this.
60292.m: Liquefied natural gas is shipped from Yamal across the Arctic.

60293.q: When did the Norse settlements in Greenland disappear?
60293.e: The Eastern and Western Settlements were gradually abandoned, the Eastern Settlement last in the 15th century. Cooling, declining trade and isolation are considered the reasons.
60293.m: The Norse settlements in Greenland came to an end in the 15th century.

60294.q: What, among other things, did Greenland receive with the Self-Government Act of 2009?
a: A seat in the EU Commission
60294.e: Since 2009 Greenland has decided for itself about raw materials such as ores and oil. The act also recognises the right of Greenlanders to decide on their independence.
60294.m: Since 2009 Greenland has managed its own mineral resources.

60295.q: What was Camp Century, built in the ice of north-west Greenland in 1959?
a: A US military base in tunnels under the ice
A Danish weather station on a glacier
An Inuit village for seal hunters
60295.e: The USA built tunnels into the ice and ran the station with a small nuclear reactor. After it was abandoned in 1967, waste remained that could be exposed by melting.
60295.m: Camp Century was a military base under the Greenland ice.

60296.q: What did Greenland's parliament decide in 2021 in the dispute over a mining project near Narsaq?
a: The sale of land to China
60296.e: At Kvanefjeld rare earths are found together with uranium. After an election, parliament banned exploring for and mining ores with higher uranium content.
60296.m: In 2021 Greenland put protecting the environment ahead of uranium mining.

60297.q: What is the Isua Greenstone Belt in south-western Greenland known for?
a: Some of the oldest rocks on Earth
The largest diamonds in the world
60297.e: The rocks in the Isua belt are about 3.7 to 3.8 billion years old. They give clues about the early Earth and possibly early life.
60297.m: Some of the oldest rocks on Earth are in the Isua belt.

60298.q: Why does the bedrock beneath the middle of Greenland lie partly below sea level?
a: The weight of the ice pushes the Earth's crust down
There is a deep ocean trench there
The rock was washed out by rivers
60298.e: The kilometres-thick ice sheet weighs down the crust, which sinks into the viscous mantle. If the ice melted, the land would slowly rise again.
60298.m: Heavy ice pushes the Earth's crust down.

60299.q: What is geologically special about Macquarie Island, which belongs to Tasmania?
a: Rock from the Earth's mantle is exposed there above sea level
Australia's only active volcano is there
The oldest granite on Earth is there
There is a glacier reaching the sea there
60299.e: The island was pushed up out of the oceanic crust at a plate boundary. That is why it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
60299.m: On Macquarie Island you can see rock from the Earth's mantle.

60300.q: Which very slow-growing conifer from Tasmania was prized for boatbuilding?
60300.e: The wood of the Huon pine contains an oil that protects it from rot. The trees grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.
60300.m: The Huon pine supplies rot-resistant wood from Tasmania.

60301.q: Which exchange system with necklaces and armbands did Bronisław Malinowski describe on the Trobriand Islands?
60301.e: In the Kula ring, necklaces travel clockwise and armbands in the opposite direction from island to island. It is mainly about prestige and relationships, not profit.
60301.m: The Kula ring is an exchange system that strengthens relationships between islands.

60302.q: Which culture with decorated pottery spread out into the Pacific from the Bismarck Archipelago from about 1500 BC?
60302.e: The Lapita people were the first to settle Fiji, Tonga and Samoa from Melanesia. They are considered the ancestors of the Polynesians.
60302.m: The Lapita culture stands at the beginning of the settlement of the remote Pacific.

60303.q: Which almost constantly active volcano on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu attracts many visitors?
60303.e: Yasur has been almost continuously active for centuries and regularly throws out glowing lava. The other volcanoes named are in Papua New Guinea.
60303.m: Yasur on Tanna is one of the most active volcanoes in Melanesia.

60304.q: Which English word comes from the Polynesian languages?
60304.e: James Cook came across the word “tapu” on Tonga; it means something sacred or forbidden. Through his reports it entered English as “taboo”.

60305.q: Which French painter lived and painted in French Polynesia from 1891?
60305.e: Gauguin painted bright pictures of island life on Tahiti and later on the Marquesas. He died in 1903 on the island of Hiva Oa.
60305.m: Paul Gauguin painted his best-known pictures in Polynesia.

60306.q: Which country does the Polynesian island of Tahiti belong to?
60306.e: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, an overseas territory of France. The capital Papeete is on Tahiti.
60306.m: Tahiti belongs to French Polynesia and therefore to France.

60307.q: What do you call a ring-shaped coral island with a lagoon in the middle, as often found in Polynesia?
60307.e: An atoll forms when a volcano with a coral reef slowly sinks. The reef keeps growing upwards and encloses a lagoon.
60307.m: An atoll is a ring of coral around a lagoon.

60308.q: Who settled the Pitcairn Islands in 1790?
a: Mutineers from the Bounty with people from Tahiti
60308.e: After the mutiny on the Bounty in 1789, some mutineers hid on Pitcairn with Tahitian women and men. Their descendants still live there today.
60308.m: The Pitcairn Islands were settled by mutineers from the Bounty.

60309.q: Which drink made from the root of a pepper plant is drunk at ceremonies in Tonga and Samoa?
60309.e: Kava is made from the ground root of the kava pepper plant mixed with water. At ceremonies it is served according to a fixed order of rank.
60309.m: Kava is a traditional ceremonial drink in Polynesia.

60310.q: Which Micronesian country became the first in 2009 to declare its waters a sanctuary for sharks?
60310.e: Palau banned commercial shark fishing in its entire economic zone. Live sharks bring the country much more through diving tourism than caught ones.
60310.m: In 2009 Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary.

60311.q: What does the “Compact of Free Association” between the USA and several Micronesian countries regulate?
a: The USA takes over defence, and citizens may work in the USA
The USA buys all fishing rights
The countries must abolish the US dollar
60311.e: The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau receive financial aid and defence. In return the USA has special military rights there.
60311.m: Through the Compact of Free Association three Micronesian countries are closely tied to the USA.

60312.q: Why is the Chuuk Lagoon a famous destination for wreck divers?
a: Dozens of Japanese ships sunk in 1944 lie there
The Bounty sank there with its cargo
60312.e: In Operation Hailstone in February 1944, US aircraft attacked the Japanese base. Many ships and aircraft still lie on the bottom of the lagoon today.
60312.m: Chuuk Lagoon is an underwater museum of the Second World War.

60313.q: Which property does the Mercator projection have?
a: It preserves distances from the centre
60313.e: The Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical projection: angles and small shapes are preserved. In exchange, areas are greatly enlarged towards the poles.
60313.m: The Mercator projection preserves angles but not areas.

60314.q: In which year did Gerardus Mercator publish his world map with the projection named after him?
60314.e: In 1569 Gerardus Mercator published a large world map for navigation in Duisburg. It is considered the origin of the Mercator projection.
60314.m: Mercator published his famous world map in 1569.

60315.q: Why was the Mercator projection especially useful for navigation at sea?
a: Lines of constant compass bearing appear as straight lines
The shortest routes appear as straight lines
The areas of the oceans are correct
The poles appear as single points
